title: Chapter 4 Mastery Quiz: Neuroplasticity & Split-Brain Research
description: Test your mastery of hemispheric specialization, surgical callosotomy, Sperry and Gazzaniga's findings, structural plasticity, Hebbian learning, and LTP.

questions.question: What is the primary anatomical structure interconnecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres?

options.text: Corpus Callosum
Internal Capsule
Fornix
Cerebellar Peduncles

questions.explanation: The corpus callosum contains 200-300 million axons bridging homologous areas of the two cerebral hemispheres.

questions.question: Approximately how many nerve fibers cross within the adult human Corpus Callosum?

options.text: 200 to 300 million fibers
10,000 fibers
1 billion fibers
500 fibers

questions.explanation: The corpus callosum is the largest white matter tract in the human brain, containing roughly 200-300 million axons.

questions.question: In the majority of humans (>90% of right-handers), which hemisphere is dominant for speech production and grammatical syntax?

options.text: Left hemisphere
Right hemisphere
Both hemispheres equally in every individual
The cerebellum

questions.explanation: Language production (Broca's area) and grammar are overwhelmingly lateralized to the left cerebral hemisphere.

questions.question: The planum temporale, an anatomical region associated with auditory language processing, is typically:

options.text: Significantly larger in the left hemisphere than in the right
Five times larger in the right hemisphere
Present only in patients with split-brain surgery
Located inside the lateral ventricles

questions.explanation: The planum temporale is significantly larger in the left hemisphere, reflecting structural specialization for language.

questions.question: For what medical condition was surgical corpus callosotomy originally developed as a treatment?

options.text: Severe, intractable, generalized epilepsy
Parkinsonian tremors
Hydrocephalus in infants
Major depressive disorder

questions.explanation: Callosotomy prevents generalization of life-threatening epileptic seizure activity from one hemisphere to the other.

questions.question: In tachistoscopic testing of split-brain patients, why must visual stimuli be flashed for less than 150 milliseconds?

options.text: To prevent eye saccades that would allow the opposite hemisphere to view the image
Because the retinas stop firing after 100 milliseconds
To avoid overheating the visual cortex
To trigger sleep spindles in the thalamus

questions.explanation: Saccadic eye movements take ~150-200 ms to initiate; flashing images faster restricts visual input to a single hemifield.

questions.question: An image flashed strictly in the Right Visual Field (RVF) projects to which hemisphere?

options.text: Left hemisphere visual cortex
Right hemisphere visual cortex
Bilateral superior colliculi only
Directly to the spinal cord

questions.explanation: Due to partial decussation at the optic chiasm, information from the right visual hemifield projects to the left visual cortex.

questions.question: When a split-brain patient is presented with an object in the Left Visual Field, why can they not name it verbally?

options.text: The visual information reaches the right hemisphere, which cannot transfer it across the severed callosum to the left-hemisphere speech center
The patient's vocal cords become temporarily paralyzed
The left eye ceases functioning during testing
The right hemisphere has no visual processing capacity

questions.explanation: The right hemisphere perceives the object, but cannot transfer data across the severed callosum to Broca's area in the left hemisphere.

questions.question: What is Gazzaniga's concept of the left-hemisphere 'Interpreter'?

options.text: A cognitive system that constructs post-hoc explanations and narratives to rationalize behaviors driven by unconscious or right-hemisphere processes
A specialized software package for transcribing audio recordings in brain surgery
A thalamic nucleus that converts French into English
A reflex arc that straightens posture during walking

questions.explanation: The Interpreter is a left-hemisphere mechanism that constructs plausible narratives to make sense of ongoing actions and inputs.

questions.question: Which of the following best exemplifies 'functional neuroplasticity'?

options.text: An undamaged area of the cortex adopting the functions previously performed by a stroke-damaged region
The formation of scar tissue that permanently prevents any nerve signaling
The growth of bone around the skull after a fracture
A heart rate increase during aerobic running

questions.explanation: Functional plasticity describes the functional reorganization of intact brain circuits to assume lost tasks following damage.

questions.question: In Eleanor Maguire's landmark MRI study of London taxi drivers, which brain structure exhibited increased gray matter volume in experienced drivers?

options.text: Posterior hippocampus
Anterior cingulate cortex
Cerebellar vermis
Occipital pole

questions.explanation: London taxi drivers showed significant structural enlargement of the posterior hippocampus, which stores mental spatial maps.

questions.question: What is the neuroanatomical explanation for phantom hand sensations evoked by touching an amputee's face?

options.text: The cortical face representation borders the hand representation on the somatosensory homunculus and invades the deafferented cortex
Nerves in the face physically grow down the neck into the shoulder stump
The amputee is consciously imagining sensations out of emotional grief
The thalamus completely dissolves after amputation

questions.explanation: Somatotopic cortical remapping causes sensory afferents from the adjacent face region to sprout into the vacant hand representation in S1.

questions.question: How does V.S. Ramachandran's 'Mirror Box' treat painful phantom limb paralysis?

options.text: It provides visual feedback of the intact limb moving, 'tricking' the brain into releasing learned motor paralysis
It delivers high-voltage electric shocks to the stump
It forces the patient to memorize 3D geometric shapes
It chemically destroys all pain nociceptors in the spinal cord

questions.explanation: Visual feedback of the reflection of the moving intact arm overcomes the sensory-motor mismatch, relieving phantom spasms.

questions.question: Donald Hebb's famous postulate (1949) is colloquially summarized by which maxim?

options.text: Neurons that fire together, wire together
Use it or lose it within thirty seconds
Structure always precedes function
All sensory modalities are created equal

questions.explanation: Hebbian plasticity states that coordinated firing of presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons strengthens their synaptic connection.

questions.question: Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) is widely recognized as the primary cellular model for:

options.text: Learning and memory formation in mammalian brains
Cell death during acute cerebral ischemia
Spinal cord reflex arcs in invertebrates
Circadian entrainment by sunlight

questions.explanation: LTP provides a long-lasting, activity-dependent increase in synaptic efficacy, serving as the biological substrate of memory.

questions.question: Why is the NMDA receptor classified as a 'molecular coincidence detector'?

options.text: It requires simultaneous glutamate binding and postsynaptic membrane depolarization to open
It opens only when two separate action potentials hit the same node of Ranvier
It detects both sound waves and light waves simultaneously
It operates in both hemispheres at the exact same microsecond

questions.explanation: NMDA channels require presynaptic glutamate binding AND postsynaptic depolarization (to dislodge the Mg2+ plug) to permit ion flux.

questions.question: Which ion entering through the open NMDA receptor acts as the key intracellular second messenger that triggers LTP?

options.text: Calcium (Ca2+)
Chloride (Cl-)
Magnesium (Mg2+)
Potassium (K+)

questions.explanation: Calcium influx activates CaMKII and other intracellular cascades that recruit and insert additional AMPA receptors into the synapse.

questions.question: What is the primary postsynaptic structural change that renders a potentiated synapse more sensitive to future glutamate release?

options.text: Insertion of additional AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane
Total destruction of all dendritic spines
Conversion of gray matter into cerebrospinal fluid
Elimination of the cell nucleus

questions.explanation: LTP recruits and inserts AMPA receptors from submembrane pools into the postsynaptic density, increasing EPSP magnitude.

questions.question: What is Long-Term Depression (LTD) in synaptic neuroscience?

options.text: An activity-dependent weakening of synaptic connections and internalization of AMPA receptors
A clinical mood disorder lasting more than two years
The complete cessation of blood flow to the temporal lobe
Loss of myelin sheaths along the spinal cord

questions.explanation: LTD is the persistent weakening of a synapse caused by low-frequency stimulation, counter-balancing LTP to reset synaptic weights.

questions.question: In which adult human brain region has neurogenesis (the birth of new functional neurons) been conclusively demonstrated?

options.text: Subgranular Zone of the Dentate Gyrus in the Hippocampus
Primary visual cortex Layer IV
Corpus callosum splenium
Dura mater lining the skull

questions.explanation: Adult neurogenesis occurs continuously in the subgranular zone of the hippocampal dentate gyrus and the subventricular zone.

questions.question: Which lifestyle factor has been shown empirically to significantly boost adult hippocampal neurogenesis in animal and human studies?

options.text: Sustained aerobic physical exercise
Severe chronic psychological stress
Chronic sleep deprivation
High daily alcohol consumption

questions.explanation: Aerobic exercise elevates BDNF (Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor) and strongly stimulates hippocampal neurogenesis.

questions.question: What is the function of retrograde messengers (such as Nitric Oxide) during Long-Term Potentiation?

options.text: Diffusing back from the postsynaptic spine to the presynaptic terminal to increase neurotransmitter release probability
Shutting down all mitochondria in the cell body
Dissolving the myelin sheath of neighboring axons
Pumping calcium completely out of the synaptic cleft

questions.explanation: Retrograde messengers like gasotransmitter Nitric Oxide (NO) travel backward across the synapse to enhance presynaptic vesicle exocytosis.
